hook.text: Your new model scores ninety-one percent on two thousand test examples. The model in production scored ninety and a half, on the same examples. Ship it?

plan.text: The statistics round asks how far to trust a number like that. Seventeen questions: twelve worked through, mostly on this decision, then five quick ones.

q1.text: Question one. What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error? Standard deviation is the spread of single observations. Each test example is right or wrong: at ninety-one percent, a spread of point two nine.

q1-se.text: Standard error is the spread of a statistic, like the accuracy, across repeated samples: the standard deviation over the square root of n. On two thousand examples, it's about two thirds of a percentage point, more than the gap.

q1-n.text: More data shrinks the standard error, never the standard deviation, and only at a square-root rate. Halving it, to a third of a point, takes eight thousand examples: four times the data.

q2.text: Question two. What does the Central Limit Theorem say, and why does it matter? For a large enough sample, the sample mean is approximately normal, whatever the population's shape, as long as its variance is finite. That justifies normal intervals and tests, even on skewed data.

q2-sim.text: The page's simulation draws three thousand samples of forty from a heavily skewed population. Their means pile up in a bell, with a spread of point four seven five, against the formula's point four seven seven.

q2-limit.text: It covers means and sums, so accuracy and average loss. For a median, or a ninety-fifth percentile latency, there's no such formula.

q3.text: Question three. What is the Law of Large Numbers, and how is it different from the CLT? The law says where the sample mean ends up: at the population mean. The CLT says what shape its error takes on the way there.

q4.text: Question four. What is a confidence interval, really? It's a procedure, not a probability about one interval: the estimate, plus or minus one point nine six standard errors, built on every repeat of an experiment, contains the true value about ninety-five percent of the time.

q4-sim.text: Simulate a hundred test sets for a model that's truly ninety-one percent accurate, and ninety-six of the hundred intervals cover it. Each one either does or doesn't; the ninety-five percent belongs to the procedure.

q4-slice.text: The follow-up is where it breaks. On a slice of forty examples, with a model that's ninety-seven percent right, three slices in ten score forty out of forty, and the textbook interval shrinks to a point. Across all slices, it covers the truth only seventy percent of the time. Wilson's score interval doesn't collapse, and covers ninety-seven.

q5.text: Question five. What is bootstrapping, and when do you use it? Resample your data with replacement, at its own size, thousands of times, recompute the statistic, and read the interval off the percentiles. No formula needed.

q5-p95.text: Take a thousand simulated request latencies. The ninety-fifth percentile is a hundred and ten milliseconds, and five thousand resamples put it between a hundred and one and a hundred and twenty.

q5-unit.text: The follow-up: resample the unit that was sampled. If two thousand test rows come from two hundred users, resampling rows treats them as independent, and the interval comes out a third too narrow. Resample whole users.

q6.text: Question six. What exactly is a p-value? The probability of data at least as extreme as yours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Small means your data would be surprising if nothing were going on.

q6-not.text: [slowly] Because it assumes the null, it can't be the probability that the null is true, or that your result is a fluke.

q7.text: Question seven. What is hypothesis testing, and what are its steps? State the null and the alternative. Fix the significance level, alpha, and the sample size, before you look. Compute a test statistic and its p-value, and reject the null if p is below alpha. Here, the null is that the two models are equally accurate.

q7-peek.text: Fixing it all in advance is what keeps the test honest. Simulate two equally good models, and check after every two hundred labels: stop at the first p under five percent, and you find a difference nineteen percent of the time, not five.

q8.text: Question eight. What is a permutation test? It builds the null distribution by shuffling the group labels, which are interchangeable if there's no effect. On the page's two groups of fifty, the difference is five point nine, and ten thousand shuffles match or beat it two point four percent of the time.

q8-models.text: Now the two models. Pool their four thousand right-or-wrong answers and shuffle, and p is point six two. Nothing there.

q8-paired.text: But they answered the same two thousand examples, and disagree on only eighteen, of which the new model wins fourteen. Shuffle within each pair instead, swapping which model gave which answer, and p is point oh three. Same gap, but the paired test uses how the data was collected, and at five percent it rejects the null.

q9.text: Question nine. What are type one and type two errors, and what is power? Type one is a false positive, rejecting a true null, at rate alpha. Type two is a false negative, missing a real effect, at rate beta. Power, one minus beta, is the chance of catching a real effect.

q9-trade.text: It rises with more data, a bigger effect, less noise, or a looser alpha. Lowering alpha trades false positives for false negatives.

q9-online.text: Whether users notice is an online test, where you choose the sample size. Catching a click rate moving from five percent to five and a half, at eighty percent power, takes about thirty-one thousand users per arm. Half that lift takes four times the users.

q9-null.text: With five thousand per arm, that lift is caught one time in five. So a test that small, which finds nothing, hasn't shown the models are equal.

q10-in.text: Every test so far trusted the sample. Next, whether it's the right one.

q10.text: Question ten. What is selection bias? The sample doesn't represent the population you want to generalize to, so estimates stay off however much data you collect. In machine learning, it's training on a population unlike your serving traffic.

q10-loans.text: In a simulation, a lender only sees defaults on the loans it approved. Among those, five point three percent default. Across every applicant, it's eleven point six percent. Sixty times as many approved loans don't close that gap.

q10-fix.text: The fix is in how the data is collected. Approve a small random slice whatever the score, here two percent, and its default rate is eleven point eight percent. The price is some bad loans, for labels you can trust.

q11.text: Question eleven. What is maximum likelihood estimation? Pick the parameters that make the observed data most probable, under your model.

q11-log.text: You maximize the log of the likelihood, because the product underflows. Give each of two thousand labels a probability of one half, and float sixty-four rounds their product to exactly zero. Its log is just minus thirteen hundred and eighty-six.

q11-loss.text: For a normal model, the likelihood peaks at the sample mean, and maximizing it is least squares. For logistic regression, it's minimizing the log loss.

q11-small.text: The catch is small samples. Three clicks in three views, and the likelihood peaks at a hundred percent. Add one pretend click and one pretend skip, a prior, and it's four in five. An L2 penalty is the same idea for weights: a normal prior on them.

q12.text: Question twelve. What is Bayes' theorem? It updates a prior belief with evidence: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, over the evidence. The classic trap is the base rate.

q12-fraud.text: Say a fraud model catches ninety-nine percent of fraud and flags one percent of honest transactions, and one in a thousand is fraud. Of a hundred thousand, it flags ninety-nine frauds and nine hundred and ninety-nine honest ones. A flag is fraud only nine percent of the time.

q12-shift.text: And precision moves with the base rate, while recall doesn't. If fraud rises to one in a hundred, the same model's flags are right half the time. Nothing in the model changed.

rapid-in.text: Five quick ones, on the vocabulary.

r-pdf.text: A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. A discrete one has a mass function: each value's probability. A continuous one has a density, where probability is area, so a single point has probability zero, and the height can pass one, as a narrow normal's does.

r-dist.text: The distributions to know: Bernoulli and binomial for yes-or-no outcomes and their counts. Normal for symmetric data, and for means. Poisson for rare-event counts, where the mean equals the variance. Uniform for equal chances, exponential for waiting times. Their supports and moments say which likelihood fits.

r-sample.text: Sampling: simple random gives every unit the same chance. Stratified samples within groups, so each one shows up, like a rare class in every test set. Cluster sampling takes whole groups, to cut cost. Reservoir sampling handles a stream.

r-corr.text: Covariance says whether two variables move together, but its size depends on their units. Correlation divides by both standard deviations, landing between minus one and one, and it only sees straight lines: y equals x squared, on a symmetric range, has a correlation of zero.

r-cause.text: And correlation isn't causation: a confounder can drive both, as hot weather drives ice cream sales and drownings. A model can predict from a correlation. Deciding what to change needs a randomized experiment, or a causal method that rules confounders out.

next.text: Minimizing log loss is maximum likelihood, and a deep network does it with millions of weights. Next: deep learning.
